bib.title: Chapter 2. Markov Decision Processes, Dynamic Programming, and Monte Carlo Methods
authors: Winder (book: Reinforcement Learning; author not printed in chapter text, taken from the directory name)

question: How do bandit testing, Markov decision processes, Monte Carlo methods and dynamic programming (value iteration) formalise and solve sequential decision problems?
contributions: Frames bandit testing as RL and introduces reward, exploration vs exploitation, epsilon-greedy, annealing-softmax and UCB.
Defines MDPs, policies, discounted return, state-value and action-value functions, optimal policies and the Bellman optimality idea.
Presents on-policy Monte Carlo control and DP value iteration, with caveats on DP.

results.claim: In the epsilon-greedy button bandit simulation, the red button is clicked by 40% of simulated users and green by 5%.
results.setup: Simulated Bernoulli users, two actions (red, green), reward 1 per click
results.quote: I assume that a whopping 40% of users click the red button, but only 5% of users click the green.

results.claim: Each epsilon-greedy simulation ran 250 steps, averaged over 1,000 repeats.
results.setup: Two-button bandit, three epsilon values compared (values not stated in text, only in Fig 2-2)
results.note: Averaged over 1,000 repeats per the text: 'on average, over 1,000 repeats'.

results.claim: With epsilon=1 the optimal-action rate asymptotes at 0.5; the stated asymptote with epsilon=0.1 is 0.95.
results.setup: Two actions; the epsilon values are lost from the extracted text (formula garbled), 0.1 is inferred from 1-eps+eps/2=0.95
results.quote: the result is an optimal action of 0.95
results.note: Epsilon symbols missing from the cached text.

results.claim: Annealing-softmax and UCB learn an optimal action far quicker than epsilon-greedy; UCB has no tunable parameters.
results.setup: Same two-button bandit; epsilon chosen to approximate the same final performance as the others (Fig 2-3)
results.quote: You can see that the annealing-softmax and the UCB strategies learn an optimal action far quicker than the -greedy method.

results.claim: Inventory example: probability of a sale per day is 0.7, restock-at-random uses probability 0.5, so random restocking loses sales; constant restocking and restock-at-zero perform about equally, with 0.7 the maximum sales proportion.
results.setup: Three states (0,1,2 items), two actions (restock, none), Bernoulli sale p=0.7, reward only on sale; three policies compared
results.quote: the probability of a sale (0.7) was greater than the probability of restocking (0.5)
results.note: Per-policy proportions appear only in the Fig 2-6 legend.

results.claim: Random-policy state-value estimation on the five-square cliff after 10,000 episodes is close to the theoretical values.
results.metric: estimated expected return for squares 1 to 4
results.setup: Random left/right policy, discount 1, reward 5 at goal, no cliff penalty
results.quote: After ten thousand random experiments the result is very close: [1.00, 1.97, 2.92, 3.92]

results.claim: The optimal policy in the cliff environment is to choose right every time, as right action values exceed left.
results.quote: the optimal policy is to choose “right” every time.

results.claim: Value-iteration hand example: up action with 80% to +1 and 20% to -1 gives expected value 0.6, versus 0 for down.
results.setup: All state values zero, one step, Fig 2-12
results.quote: The expected value for the current state is 0.6.

results.claim: Value iteration on the cliff problem with discount 0.9 gives the same policy as MC, with values rising toward the goal.
results.setup: Five-square cliff problem, Algorithm 2-4, results in Fig 2-13
results.quote: A discount factor of 0.9 was used to find the optimal policy for the simple cliff problem encountered earlier.

results.claim: Typical discount rates in nontrivial problems are between 0.9 and 0.99.
results.quote: In most nontrivial examples the discount rate is set between 0.9 and 0.99.

results.claim: DP can improve a policy faster than MC because MC must wait for episode end, but DP needs a model, discounting, and sweeps over all states.
results.quote: DP can improve a policy much faster than MC, which is very important when dealing with problems with long (or infinite) episodes.

limits: Toy simulations only (two-button bandit, 3-state inventory, 5-square cliff); no real data or benchmarks.
Epsilon values for Fig 2-2 and the per-policy sales proportions appear only in figures, not in the text.
Author states four DP caveats: needs discounting, computationally prohibitive for many states, needs sample from every state-action pair, needs transition probabilities.
Claims most RL algorithms assume normally distributed rewards so the expectation is the sample mean, which hides reward distribution nuances (distributional RL).
Inventory example is acknowledged as hypothetical: restocking is instant and free, so the reward gives no ordering cost.
practices: Keep the reward quantitative and as simple as possible, since complex rewards let algorithms exploit flaws (Reward Engineering).
Test candidate policies against baselines, e.g. three restocking policies (Inventory Control Simulation).
Build simple simulators to test RL algorithms; they need not be complex (Simulating the Environment).
Anneal epsilon over time, or use UCB to avoid tuning epsilon (Improving the epsilon-greedy Algorithm).
Stick to maximising return to avoid confusion (Optimal Policies tip).
Use several different environments to avoid overfitting an algorithm to one simulation (Simulation using the state-value function tip).
Turn a POMDP back into an MDP by feeding information from previous time steps into the current one (Inventory Control Simulation).
Form a hypothesis about expected results before running an experiment (tip in state-value section).

terms.definition: A mathematical formalism in which an agent influences a stochastic system (the environment) by choosing actions; next state and reward depend only on the previous state and the action.
The total reward from the current step up to the final time step (or infinity), discounted by a factor between 0 and 1.
A mapping from states to potential actions; formally the probability of choosing an action given a state.
The expected return starting from a state and following a policy.
terms.where: Predicting Rewards with the State-Value Function

terms.definition: The expected return for a state and action under a policy, like a two-dimensional lookup table.
terms.where: Predicting Rewards with the Action-Value Function

terms.definition: A policy that, when followed, generates the highest possible expected return.
Samples full trajectories and estimates the policy's value while using it to select actions.
Estimates the action value as the average of returns from the first visit to the state-action pair in an episode; every-visit uses all visits and is noisier.
Combining policy evaluation and policy improvement, interleaved at different levels.
A DP technique that sweeps all states, taking the max over actions of the expected reward plus next state value, until error falls below a threshold, then outputs a deterministic greedy policy.
With probability epsilon take a random action, otherwise the action with highest average reward.
terms.where: Policy Improvement: Choosing the Best Action

terms.definition: Reducing the value of epsilon over time.
Upper-confidence-bound methods add a bonus to actions with inadequately sampled states, with no epsilon hyperparameter.
Partially observable MDP: an extra mapping between observations and the actual state.
